newsitem.title: CANADA: Newfoundland premier could cut Hydro-Quebec power.
newsitem.headline: Newfoundland premier could cut Hydro-Quebec power.

text.p: The premier of Newfoundland has threatened to switch off the huge Churchill Falls hydroelectric project in Labrador if Quebec does not pay more for the 4,300 megawatts it buys, the Globe and Mail newspaper reported on Saturday.
Premier Brian Tobin told Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard of his plan during a recent premiers' conference in Jasper Alberta, the Toronto newspaper reported, citing an unnamed, well-placed source.

Under the terms of a 65-year contract negotiated in the 1960s, Newfoundland sells power from Churchill Falls to provincial utility Hydro-Quebec, which resells it to customers in Quebec and the United States for about 10 times more.
Newfoundland gets from C$70 million to C$80 million a year from the deal while Hydro-Quebec will earn C$750 million this year, Newfoundland government figures show.
The price Quebec pays to Newfoundland is due to drop in 2001 and again in 2016. The contract runs until 2041.

"It isn't fair. It isn't right. It isn't moral," the Globe quoted Tobin as saying in an interview Friday. "There's nothing decent about this. And fundamental human decency requires that the circumstances be adjusted to provide a fair return to Hydro-Quebec and a fair return to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador.
"This is what is required and that is what must occur. And it will in one fashion or another."
Previous attempts by Newfoundland to force Quebec to renegotiate the arrangement have failed, including a decision by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1988 that favored Quebec.

The Globe said that before he shuts off power from the project, of which Newfoundland owns two-thirds and Hydro-Quebec one-third, Tobin plans to launch a national campaign to build public support for his province and put pressure on Quebec.
Tobin noted that the cost of running Churchill Falls will outstrip his province's profits by the year 2000.

"Honestly, what choice do I have?" he said. "Am I going to explain to the province that we're losing money and for the next 40 years we'll borrow, tax and close down hospitals and schools in the province to pay for the privilege of pumping power to Quebec so they can make a billion-plus a year?"

Tobin was elected Liberal premier of his province, Canada's poorest, earlier this year after earning international fame as the national fisheries minister. He launched a high-powered campaign against over-fishing in the Atlantic that targeted Spanish fishermen and raised tensions with the European Union, until a deal was struck last year.
